followUps:
Return an id immediately, then let the client learn the result in one of three ways. Polling: respond 202 Accepted with a job id; the client calls GET /jobs/{id} every few seconds. Simple, works everywhere, but wastes calls. Webhook: the server calls a URL the client registered, good for server-to-server; sign the request and retry on failure. WebSocket or SSE push: best for browsers needing instant updates, but needs connection management.

Example: 1,000 clients polling every 5 s is 200 requests/s of mostly empty answers; push needs only 1,000 open connections.

The queue fixes some problems and creates new ones. Duplicates: at-least-once delivery means a message can arrive twice, so consumers must be idempotent. Reordering: retries and parallel consumers can shuffle messages. Lag: if input is faster than consumers, the backlog grows and users wait. Poison messages block or loop forever without a dead-letter queue. Lost messages if the queue is not durable or the producer does not wait for the ack.

Also new: eventual consistency (the user sees stale data for a moment) and one more system to monitor. Watch queue depth and oldest-message age.

Pick SQS or RabbitMQ when you need a simple work queue and do not need replay. SQS: fully managed, no brokers to run, per-message acks with visibility timeout, built-in DLQ, scales without planning partitions. RabbitMQ: rich routing (topic and header exchanges), priorities, per-message TTL and delay, request/reply. Kafka needs partition planning and more operations, and its consumers cannot exceed the partition count.

Example: 200 jobs/s of image resizing with retries fits SQS and costs almost no operations; Kafka would be overkill.

SNS plus SQS fan-out means one published event reaches many independent queues. A publisher sends one message to an SNS topic; each interested service has its own SQS queue subscribed to that topic, so each gets a copy and processes it at its own pace with its own retries and DLQ.

OrderPlaced -> SNS topic
   -> SQS billing-queue   -> billing workers
   -> SQS email-queue     -> email workers
   -> SQS analytics-queue -> analytics workers

If email is down, only its queue grows; billing is unaffected. Unlike Kafka, a new subscriber cannot replay old events.

Unclean leader election means promoting a replica that is not in the ISR (it missed some records) to leader when every in-sync replica is gone. It restores availability but loses data: records the old leader had acknowledged and the new one lacks are silently discarded, and offsets can diverge. It is controlled by unclean.leader.election.enable, off by default.

Example: leader has offsets 0-100, the lagging follower only 0-90. After an unclean election, 91-100 are lost. Keep it off for payments; consider it for lossy metrics where uptime matters more.

Kafka is fast because it does the cheap thing everywhere. Sequential I/O: appending to a log and reading in order is fast even on disks (hundreds of MB/s). Page cache: the OS keeps recent data in RAM, so tail reads rarely hit disk. Batching and compression: many records per request, fewer round trips. Zero-copy (sendfile): bytes go from page cache to the network card without copying through the JVM.

Example: batching 500 records of 1 KB into one 500 KB compressed request costs one round trip instead of 500.

Do not add partitions to the live topic if ordering matters; create a new topic and migrate. Steps: (1) create orders-v2 with the new count; (2) have producers write to both, or run a copier that re-keys old records into v2; (3) let consumers drain v1 per key, then switch them to v2; (4) stop v1 writers and delete v1 later.

Why: the partition is hash(key) % N, so going from 6 to 12 partitions moves many keys, and a key's new events may be processed before its old ones. The new topic gives a clean cutover point.

Tiered storage moves old log segments to cheap object storage, so disk size on brokers stops limiting retention. Sizing then depends less on how long you keep data and more on throughput and the hot window kept locally. You can keep weeks of history with small broker disks, and rebuilding a broker is quicker because only the local tail is copied.

Example: 100 MB/s with 7 days retention is about 60 TB per copy; keeping only 6 hours locally needs about 2 TB per copy. Partition count is still set by throughput and consumer parallelism; old-data reads are slower, so replays take longer.

code.title: At-least-once delivery with idempotent processing
code.python:
import sqlite3

# The broker redelivers evt-2 because a crash happened before the offset commit.
messages = [("evt-1", 100), ("evt-2", 50), ("evt-2", 50), ("evt-3", 25)]
print("deliveries:", messages)

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE processed(event_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY)")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE balance(total INTEGER)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO balance VALUES (0)")

def handle(event_id, amount):
    try:
        # One transaction: the dedupe row and the effect commit together
        with db:
            db.execute("INSERT INTO processed VALUES (?)", (event_id,))
            db.execute("UPDATE balance SET total = total + ?", (amount,))
        return "applied"
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
        # Primary key already exists: we have seen this event id
        return "duplicate skipped"

naive = 0
for event_id, amount in messages:
    naive += amount  # no dedupe: the duplicate is counted twice
    print(event_id, handle(event_id, amount))

total = db.execute("SELECT total FROM balance").fetchone()[0]
print("naive total:", naive)        # 225 (wrong)
print("idempotent total:", total)   # 175 (right)

followUps:
Because a sender can never tell whether a lost ack means the message was lost or only the reply. After a timeout it must choose: resend (maybe a duplicate) or not resend (maybe a loss). This is the Two Generals problem: no finite exchange of messages makes both sides certain.

So systems choose at-least-once delivery and make the effect idempotent, which gives exactly-once processing. Example: a payment resent with the same id charges once because the second attempt finds the id already recorded.

Generate it as early as possible, at the origin of the intent, and keep it stable across every retry. For a payment, the client or the order service creates a payment_id (a UUID, or a hash of order id plus attempt purpose) before the first call and stores it with the order. Do not generate it inside the consumer or per attempt, because then every retry looks like a new request.

Pass the same value as the Idempotency-Key to the payment provider, and keep it as a unique key in your own table. Two clicks on Pay therefore share one key.

The consumer is kicked out of the group, and its batch is redone by someone else. If processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 minutes) the broker assumes the consumer is stuck, triggers a rebalance and gives its partitions away; the late commit then fails with CommitFailedException and the batch is processed twice.

Fixes: lower max.poll.records so each batch is quick, raise the interval only as a last resort, or hand slow work to a worker pool while the poll loop keeps polling (using pause()). A 10-minute batch is better split into 1-minute pieces with idempotent handlers.

Autoscaling changes group membership, so every scale event causes a rebalance, and a flapping autoscaler causes a rebalance storm. Also, extra consumers beyond the partition count sit idle, so scaling past it helps nothing.

Mitigations: use cooperative or KIP-848 rebalancing so only moved partitions pause; scale on lag with a long cooldown and gradual steps; cap max replicas at the partition count; use static membership so a rolling restart does not rebalance. Example: 12 partitions and a cap of 12 pods, scaling up by 2 pods at most every 5 minutes.

code.title: Keyed partitioning and per-order version check

followUps:
Then no single service owns the order, so you must make order explicit rather than hope. Options: route both services' events for that order through the same topic and key (orderId), so the broker order is the order; or give each event a per-order version or causal id, and let consumers apply only the next expected version, parking or rejecting others.

Better still, let one service own the order lifecycle and have the other send commands to it. Example: payment emits v3 while shipping emits v2; the consumer sees v3 first, parks it, applies v2, then v3. Timestamps alone are unsafe because clocks differ.

Retry topics break ordering, because a failed event moves aside while later events of the same key continue on the main topic. Event 2 then retries after event 3 has been applied.

Options: if ordering matters, park the key: when an event of key K goes to retry, later events for K also go to retry (or wait) until it succeeds; or block the partition and retry in place with backoff (simple, but one bad message stalls the partition); or make handlers version-aware so a late event 2 is ignored when version 3 is already applied. Choose by how costly a stall is versus a wrong state.

code.title: Retry with backoff and a dead-letter queue

followUps:
Use delay topics or a due-time check instead of Thread.sleep, because sleeping inside the poll loop triggers a rebalance after max.poll.interval.ms. Pattern: a retry topic per delay (retry-1m, retry-10m). Each record carries a not-before timestamp header. The retry consumer reads a record; if it is too early it calls pause() on that partition, keeps polling (so heartbeats continue) and resumes when the time arrives.

Because records in one retry topic have the same delay, they are already ordered by due time. Alternatives: a scheduler or database table of due messages.

If the failure happens inside poll(), the consumer cannot even hand you the record, and it retries the same offset forever. Avoid it by deserializing in your own code: configure the consumer with a ByteArrayDeserializer, then parse in a try/catch. On failure, send the raw bytes plus topic, partition and offset to the DLQ and commit past it.

Alternatively use Spring's ErrorHandlingDeserializer, which turns the failure into a marker value you can route. As a last resort, seek() to offset+1. Alert on any DLQ growth so the bad producer is fixed.

code.title: Backpressure: backlog growth and drain time
code.python:
# Lag simulation: consumers handle 1000 msgs/min, normal input is 800/min.
CAPACITY = 1000
NORMAL = 800
BURST = 5 * NORMAL      # 4000/min for 10 minutes
BURST_MINUTES = 10

lag = 0
minute = 0
for minute in range(1, BURST_MINUTES + 1):
    lag += BURST - CAPACITY          # queue grows by the surplus
print("lag after burst:", lag)       # 30000

# After the burst only the spare capacity (CAPACITY - NORMAL) drains the lag
spare = CAPACITY - NORMAL
drain = 0
while lag > 0:
    lag -= spare
    drain += 1
print("spare capacity per minute:", spare)
print("minutes to drain:", drain)    # 150

# Utilisation: 800/1000 = 80%; at 95% the drain would take far longer
for util in (0.5, 0.8, 0.95):
    spare_u = CAPACITY * (1 - util)
    print("utilisation", util, "-> drain minutes", round(30000 / spare_u))

followUps:
The queue drains slowly, because only the spare capacity works off the backlog. Burst rate = 5 x normal. With normal input 800/min, capacity 1,000/min: burst is 4,000/min, so backlog grows by 3,000/min and after 10 minutes is 30,000. Afterwards spare capacity is 200/min, so drain time is 30,000 / 200 = 150 minutes.

backlog = (burst - capacity) * burstMinutes
drain   = backlog / (capacity - normal)

Lesson: a burst of 10 minutes causes 2.5 hours of delay. Add consumers temporarily, or the drain time falls: with 2,000/min capacity it is 30,000/1,200 = 25 minutes.

Because queueing delay explodes as utilisation approaches 100%. At 75% busy there is 25% spare capacity to absorb bursts and drain backlog; at 95% there is only 5% spare, so any backlog takes 5 times longer than at 75% to clear, and latency becomes erratic.

Example: a 30,000 message backlog with 1,000/min capacity drains in 30,000 / 250 = 120 minutes at 75% utilisation but 30,000 / 50 = 600 minutes at 95%. Headroom also covers failures: if one of four consumers dies, the other three must absorb its share, so you plan for losing one instance.

code.title: Transactional outbox with a polling relay
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT)")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE outbox(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT, payload TEXT, published INTEGER DEFAULT 0)")

def place_order(order_id, fail=False):
    try:
        with db:  # one local transaction: state change + event row
            db.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, 'PLACED')", (order_id,))
            db.execute("INSERT INTO outbox(payload) VALUES (?)", ("OrderPlaced:%d" % order_id,))
            if fail:
                raise RuntimeError("crash before commit")
        print("order", order_id, "committed")
    except RuntimeError as e:
        print("order", order_id, "rolled back:", e)  # neither row exists

place_order(1)
place_order(2, fail=True)
place_order(3)

def relay():
    # Poller: publish unpublished rows in id order, then mark them
    rows = db.execute("SELECT id, payload FROM outbox WHERE published = 0 ORDER BY id").fetchall()
    for row_id, payload in rows:
        print("publish to broker:", payload)   # at-least-once: crash here => re-publish
        db.execute("UPDATE outbox SET published = 1 WHERE id = ?", (row_id,))
    db.commit()

relay()
relay()  # second run finds nothing new
print("orders:", db.execute("SELECT id FROM orders").fetchall())

followUps:
Make the outbox row carry the aggregate id and an increasing sequence, and publish with the aggregate id as the Kafka key. Rows from one transaction are then published in id order into the same partition, so consumers see that aggregate's events in the order they were committed.

Pitfall: with a poller and several relay instances, two instances could publish rows of the same aggregate out of order; use SKIP LOCKED carefully or run one relay per shard of aggregates. Also note that auto-increment ids can commit out of order across transactions, so use the per-aggregate version for ordering. CDC reading the log keeps commit order naturally.

Delete or archive rows once they are published and a safety delay has passed, otherwise the table grows forever and polling gets slow. Options: a periodic job such as DELETE FROM outbox WHERE published_at < now() - interval '7 days' in small batches; time-based partitions you drop whole (instant, no vacuum pain); or with CDC delete the row in the same transaction after insert, because the log already captured it.

DELETE FROM outbox
 WHERE published = true
   AND published_at < now() - interval '7 days'
 LIMIT 1000;

Keep a short retention to debug and to redrive.

code.title: Saga with compensations in reverse order

followUps:
You cannot unsend it, so you compensate with a correction and design the flow to avoid needing it. Send a follow-up email such as "Ignore our previous message, your order was cancelled", and record that it was sent. Better, place irreversible steps last in the saga so they run only after everything risky has succeeded, or delay the email a few minutes behind a pending state.

Example: order saga steps are reserve stock, charge card, create shipment, then send confirmation email. If the shipment fails, the email has not been sent yet and nothing needs compensating. This is called a pivot step: after it there is no rollback.

Store the saga state in durable storage, never in memory: a row per saga instance (id, current step, status, data) in a database, or in a workflow engine such as Temporal or Step Functions that persists every step. After each step the state is saved before the next command is sent.

On restart, a recovery process loads unfinished sagas and resumes from the saved step, or replays the history. Because the resumed step may already have run, every command and compensation must be idempotent, keyed by saga id plus step. Add timeouts so a saga waiting forever for a reply gets compensated.

When throughput is modest (say under a few hundred jobs per second) and you already run Postgres. A table of jobs plus SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 10 lets many workers claim different rows without blocking each other, and the claim, the work record and the business data can share one transaction. There is no new system to run, and you can query and fix jobs with SQL.

SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE status='new'
 ORDER BY id LIMIT 10
 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

Move to a real broker when load, fan-out or replay needs outgrow it.

Share groups (Kafka 4.x) give Kafka real queue behaviour. Consumers in a share group can exceed the partition count, because records of one partition are handed to several consumers, each record is acknowledged individually, and failed records are redelivered. This removes the old limit that a group can have no more active consumers than partitions, and head-of-line blocking from one slow record.

So Kafka now competes better with SQS and RabbitMQ for job queues, and you get that plus retention. Trade-off: no ordering across consumers within a partition, so use them for independent tasks, not per-key order.

code.title: Idempotent producer: sequence numbers drop duplicates

followUps:
A zombie producer is an old instance that the system thinks is dead but that is still running and writing, for example after a long GC pause or network partition. Its writes could duplicate those of its replacement. Kafka fences it with an epoch: each time a producer registers with the same transactional.id, the coordinator increments the epoch.

Example: the old instance has epoch 4, the new one gets epoch 5. The broker rejects any request with epoch 4 (ProducerFencedException), so the zombie cannot write or commit and its open transaction is aborted.

Kafka Streams keeps state (for example counts) in a local store backed by a changelog topic. Each state update is written to the changelog inside the same transaction as the output records and the input offsets. After a crash, the task restarts, reads the changelog from the beginning (or from a local checkpoint) and rebuilds the store, reading only committed records (read_committed), so aborted updates are ignored.

Standby replicas keep a warm copy so the rebuild is short. Without them, restoring a 50 GB store may take minutes. Result: state, outputs and offsets stay consistent.

Treat it as a replay into a new, versioned index, and switch over when it is ready. Never overwrite in place, because vectors from different models are not comparable. Steps: create index-v2; run a batch job reading document ids from storage (or replaying the topic) through the new model at the provider's rate limit; write with key docId+chunk+modelVersion; send live uploads to both indexes during the migration; then flip the read alias to v2 and delete v1.

Cost example: 100M docs x 5 chunks = 500M embeddings; at 5,000/s that takes about 28 hours, so budget time and money.

Deletes must travel the same pipeline as writes, otherwise stale vectors keep answering searches. Emit a DocumentDeleted{docId, version} event on the same keyed topic, so it is ordered after the upload events. The embedding consumer deletes every chunk of that docId, using a metadata filter on docId.

Guard against races: a late upload event processed after the delete would resurrect the document, so store a tombstone or compare versions and ignore anything older than the delete. Run a periodic reconciliation job comparing the document store with the index, and mark vectors as deleted in a filter immediately for privacy.

You trade parallelism for order, so one partition and one writer, tuned to be extremely fast. 1M events/s of 200 bytes is 200 MB/s, which one well-built log can write if you batch. Techniques: group commit (fsync once per batch of thousands), a single-threaded sequencer with a lock-free ring buffer (as in the LMAX design), replicate with a consensus log (Raft) for failover, and keep consumers reading in parallel afterwards.

Alternative: assign sequence numbers from a sequencer in ranges, shard by key and merge in order downstream. Plan for failover time of a few seconds.

Hybrid logical clocks (HLC) are timestamps that stay close to real time yet respect cause and effect. An HLC is a pair (physical time, counter). On each local event or message receive: take max of your clock, the received timestamp and the wall clock, and bump the counter if the physical part did not move.

Example: node A stamps (100, 0) and sends; node B's wall clock is 98, so B stamps (100, 1) for its next event. B's event sorts after A's, even though B's clock is behind. This gives a consistent order across machines without a single sequencer, though concurrent events are ordered arbitrarily.
